strengths: The core idea—discarding the encoder and directly optimizing manifold-valued latents via Riemannian optimization (building on the Deep Generative Decoder)—is simple, elegant, and immediately compatible with any manifold implemented in geoopt, sidestepping the need for closed-form densities/normalizing constants that complicate VAE-style approaches on curved spaces.

The geometry-aware noise regularization is derived cleanly from a second-order Taylor/Bishop-style analysis and is shown (Appendix E, Figure S2) to meaningfully adapt to local curvature, giving an interpretable knob relating noise scale and manifold curvature.

The paper evaluates on three diverse, well-motivated real/synthetic datasets (cell-cycle scRNA-seq, synthetic hierarchical branching diffusion, human mitochondrial DNA haplogroups), which is a nice showcase of applicability across bioinformatics/geometric-structure problems.

Reproducibility effort is good: detailed appendices document training pseudocode, hyperparameters, hardware, dataset construction, and additional ablations (noise vs. curvature sweeps, error bars), and code/data availability is mentioned.

The paper is honest about several limitations, e.g., explicitly noting that test-time comparisons are biased in favor of their model due to re-optimizing latents at test time, and discussing memory/scalability concerns of the encoder-free design.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim—that respecting the correct manifold geometry substantially improves the learned representation—is only weakly supported at test time. The authors themselves note test results are 'generally similar across methods' (Table 1) and that Euclidean spaces sometimes match or beat the specialized manifolds (e.g., Euclidean R^3 in Table 1, Euclidean R^2/Sphere with c=0.0 in Table 2 training rows), undermining the motivation for manifold-specific modeling.

The test-time evaluation protocol re-optimizes latents by maximizing log-likelihood while freezing the decoder, which the authors admit biases the comparison in favor of their own (encoder-free) model relative to encoder-based baselines (S-VAE, ΔVAE, P-VAE); this makes the reported test superiority not a fair apples-to-apples comparison.

Because each latent is a free parameter (no encoder, no amortization), the strong training-set correlations/reconstruction numbers could partly reflect memorization/overfitting rather than genuinely better geometric structure, and this is not clearly disentangled from genuine generalization improvements in the test metrics.

Quantitative structure-preservation metrics are limited to Pearson/Spearman correlation between manifold and reference distances and simple reconstruction error (MAE/MSE/F1); no more rigorous manifold-embedding quality metrics (e.g., trustworthiness, continuity, tree-distortion measures) are used, and many differences between models fall within one standard deviation of each other, weakening claims of significance.

No baseline outside VAE-style manifold models is considered (e.g., classical hyperbolic embedding methods, other manifold-learning techniques for hierarchies), and no computational-cost/scalability comparison against baselines is provided despite scalability being flagged as a concern.

Some central results are qualitative/visual (UMAP vs. Poincaré plots) rather than quantitatively validated, and the paper acknowledges the current work lacks strict benchmarking with ground-truth-labeled synthetic data, leaving open how well the approach would generalize beyond the three case studies chosen.

strengths: Simple, clean unifying idea: extend the encoder-free Deep Generative Decoder to arbitrary Riemannian manifolds by combining Riemannian (per-sample) latent optimization with standard neural decoders, avoiding intractable manifold densities/normalizing constants required by VAE-style approaches (vMF, wrapped normal, etc.).

The geometry-aware noise regularization is derived with a clear, principled second-order Taylor argument connecting Gaussian noise injection (scaled by the inverse metric) to an implicit Jacobian-based penalty tied to local curvature; this is a nice theoretical contribution distinguishing it from prior curvature-regularization work (Lee & Park, 2023) while avoiding expensive Hessian-vector computations.

Reasonably broad empirical validation across three qualitatively different domains (synthetic branching tree, cell-cycle scRNA-seq, human mtDNA haplogroups) with both qualitative visualizations and quantitative correlation/reconstruction/downstream-task metrics, plus sensible baselines (S-VAE, ΔVAE, P-VAE).

Strong scalability/practicality story: Table 4 shows the method remains stable and fast as latent dimension grows to 500D, while VAE baselines and explicit curvature regularization break down or become infeasible — a meaningful practical advantage given real single-cell data has many genes/dimensions.

Reasonably thorough appendices covering training details, manifold list (via geoopt), ablations on noise scale vs. curvature, and additional downstream/generative-fidelity checks, supporting reproducibility; a reproducibility statement and code/data links are provided.
Honest treatment of limitations (memory growth with dataset size due to per-sample latents, lack of amortized inference, generative properties not the focus) rather than glossing over them.
weaknesses: Central quantitative results are mixed/marginal: in Table 1 (cell cycle) the proposed model's correlations and reconstruction errors are essentially statistically indistinguishable from S-VAE/ΔVAE baselines, undermining the claim of a clear empirical advantage in that case; the paper's main selling point ends up being scalability/stability rather than accuracy.

The novelty over Schuster & Krogh (2023)'s Deep Generative Decoder is somewhat incremental: the core contribution is essentially swapping Euclidean free-parameter latents for Riemannian-manifold latents via an off-the-shelf Riemannian optimizer (geoopt/RiemannianAdam), which, while useful, is a relatively small conceptual step; the paper could better delineate what specifically is technically novel versus straightforward composition of existing tools (geoopt, DGD, noise-as-regularization ideas from Bishop/An).

The evaluation lacks statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests) despite reporting means ± std over only 3-5 seeds, making it hard to assess whether reported differences (e.g., Table 1, Table 2) are meaningful versus noise, especially given overlapping error bars in several rows.

No direct comparison against amortized encoder-based general-geometry VAEs beyond the specific manifold cases studied (e.g., general Riemannian normal / wrapped-normal approaches like Kalatzis et al. 2020, Falorsi et al. 2018), despite the introduction motivating the work partly against 'general geometries' methods; only S-VAE (sphere), P-VAE/ΔVAE (hyperbolic) are compared, leaving the 'any manifold' unifying claim somewhat under-tested for genuinely heterogeneous/product manifolds beyond the toy torus case.

Test-time latent inference (freezing decoder, optimizing z via MAP) is compute-intensive per new sample and is not benchmarked for cost/quality versus a trained encoder at test time, which is an important practical trade-off for an 'encoder-less' method that is not fully explored quantitatively.

The claimed geometric interpretability/superiority of the learned manifold representations relies heavily on qualitative visual inspection (e.g., Figures 2-4) and correlation to somewhat noisy proxy ground truths (one-hot mutation distance, inferred cell-cycle phase from a separate model), which are imperfect ground truths and could bias conclusions in the paper's favor.

Ablation in Section 4.2/Figure 3c shows a clear tradeoff where increasing noise beyond ~0.9 degrades reconstruction (MSE rises sharply) even as correlation improves, and the paper does not provide a principled method for selecting sigma other than manual tuning per dataset, which weakens the 'plug-and-play' scalability narrative and could limit reproducibility across new datasets without careful hyperparameter search.
